lesson.title: If It Comes to Mind Easily, It Must Be Common: The Availability Heuristic
lesson.summary: The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut in which people judge how frequent or likely an event is based on how easily examples of it come to mind, a cue that is usually helpful but can be badly distorted by memorable, vivid, or recently encountered examples.
lesson.body:
The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut for estimating how common or likely something is based on a simple, fast cue: how easily relevant examples come to mind. If instances of an event are easy to recall quickly, the event feels common or probable; if instances are hard to recall or nothing comes to mind at all, the event feels rare or unlikely. This works reasonably well much of the time because genuinely common events usually do generate more memorable instances than rare ones do, since an actually frequent experience naturally leaves more traces in memory than an actually rare one. The problem is that ease of recall is influenced by more than just true frequency.

Ease of recall is also strongly shaped by how vivid, emotional, recent, or heavily publicized an example is, independent of how often that type of event actually occurs. A dramatic plane crash covered extensively across news and social media becomes far easier to call to mind than the routine, unremarkable safety of the vast majority of flights that land without incident, which receive no coverage at all because nothing happened. As a result, people often estimate the danger of flying as higher than the danger of a statistically far more common cause of harm, such as driving a car, precisely because vivid, emotionally striking plane crash stories are so much more available in memory than the far larger number of ordinary, uneventful car trips that never make the news.

A simple illustrative scenario shows how this plays out even with small, testable judgments. Asked whether more English words begin with the letter r or have r as their third letter, most people confidently guess that more words begin with r. Words that start with a given letter are much easier to retrieve from memory, since memory is commonly organized and searched by first letter, so they feel more available, even though, by most counts, there are actually more words with r as the third letter. Nothing about the true frequency changed; only the ease of retrieval did, and that ease alone was enough to produce a confident, and incorrect, estimate.

Like the representativeness heuristic, the availability heuristic works by substituting an easy question, how easily do examples come to mind, for a harder one, how frequent or probable is this actually, a pattern common to many mental shortcuts. This substitution is efficient because ease of recall is genuinely correlated with real frequency often enough to be useful as a quick estimate, saving the enormous effort that a fully accurate statistical calculation would require. But the same substitution means that anything that makes certain examples unusually memorable, extensive media coverage, a personally frightening experience, a vivid story told by a friend, can throw off frequency judgments substantially, leading people to overestimate rare but dramatic risks and underestimate common but unremarkable ones.

Both representativeness and availability are heuristics aimed at judging probability and frequency, but not every mental shortcut is about probability at all. Some shortcuts instead involve sticking with a strategy that has worked before, even once it stops being the best available option, a pattern of thinking known as mental set.
